# Contractor vs Part-Time Employee for 20 Hours/Week Marketing Work

A practical way to review this is to compare the role against **control, independence, duration, and administration**. For California, the key issue is not the title you use, but how the work is actually performed.

## Side-by-Side Review Checklist

| Factor | Contractor | Part-Time Employee | What to Review |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classification risk | Higher if work looks ongoing, integrated, and supervised | Lower if role is clearly payroll-based | Marketing work often involves regular weekly output, which can look employee-like |
| Control over work | You should focus on results, not day-to-day direction | You can direct schedule, methods, tools, and priorities | Who decides when, how, and with what tools the work is done? |
| Documentation | Contract, scope, invoice terms, deliverables, IP terms | Offer letter, handbook acknowledgments, payroll forms | Paperwork should match the actual working relationship |
| Tax/admin burden | Usually lighter payroll burden, but more contractor setup and invoice handling | More payroll, withholding, wage/hour, and recordkeeping | Compare payroll processing, workers’ comp, and reporting needs |
| Work integration | Risk rises if work is core to daily operations | More natural if the role is part of normal staff workflow | Content creation, ad management, and weekly reporting may be tightly integrated |
| Schedule and duration | Better for project-based or limited engagements | Better for recurring, ongoing work | 20 hours/week for 6 months can look like a continuing role |
| Tools and systems | Contractor ideally uses own tools/processes where practical | Employee typically uses company tools and systems | Access to ad accounts, brand assets, and internal calendars matters |
| Supervision and performance | Limited oversight, defined deliverables | Ongoing supervision, coaching, and performance management | Weekly reporting can indicate ongoing management |
| Payment structure | Fixed project fee or milestone-based is often cleaner | Hourly or salaried payroll is standard | Consider whether pay is tied to output or time worked |
| IP and confidentiality | Must be clearly written into the agreement | Usually covered by employment docs and policy | Make sure ownership of content, ad assets, and analytics reports is explicit |

## Practical Decision Framework

### Lean toward contractor if most of these are true
- The work is **project-based** with clear deliverables.
- The person can choose **how** to complete the work.
- They use **their own tools** and work independently.
- You care mainly about **results**, not hours or process.
- The engagement is limited and not part of a permanent staffing model.

### Lean toward part-time employee if most of these are true
- You need **ongoing weekly marketing support**.
- You want to control **schedule, methods, priorities, and revisions**.
- The person will work closely inside your team and systems.
- The role is part of your regular operations, not a standalone project.
- You expect continued work after the initial period.

### For this specific work pattern
- **Content creation + ad management + weekly reporting** tends to involve regular coordination and ongoing oversight.
- **20 hours/week for 6 months** can resemble a continuing part-time role more than a one-off project.
- That does not decide the issue by itself, but it is a meaningful risk factor to review with counsel or a payroll/tax professional.

## Documentation and Admin Checklist

- **If contractor**
  - Written independent contractor agreement
  - Clear scope of work and deliverables
  - Payment terms tied to milestones or invoices
  - Confidentiality and IP ownership terms
  - Proof of business status and W-9 collection
  - Process for approving extra work or scope changes

- **If part-time employee**
  - Offer letter and job description
  - Payroll setup and tax withholding
  - Wage/hour compliance review
  - Timekeeping process
  - Handbook and policy acknowledgments
  - Workers’ compensation coverage and required postings

## California-Specific Risk Points to Review

- Whether the role satisfies the state’s **independent contractor classification test** under current law and related exceptions.
- Whether the worker is performing tasks **within the usual course** of your business.
- Whether the worker is **independently established** in the same type of marketing work.
- Whether the company is exercising control beyond a true vendor relationship.
